title: How Babies Crack Language
objective: After this level you can explain how infants pick out words and why language is easiest to learn early.
summary: Babies find words by tracking which sounds follow which, and start out hearing many languages' sounds. An early start gives a lasting edge in grammar.

cards.headline: Nobody hands a baby a dictionary. So how do babies find the words?
cards.body: Adults hear speech as separate words, but to a baby it arrives as fluent, running sound. Finding where one word ends and the next begins is a basic task of learning a language. Babies manage it anyway, and research shows both how they do it and why starting early helps.

cards.headline: Babies who keep score
cards.body: In 1996, Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin and Elissa Newport tested whether 8-month-old infants could pull words out of fluent speech. The only clue was statistical: which sounds tended to follow which. After just 2 minutes of listening, the babies could pick out the words. Nobody explained anything to them. Infants, it seems, keep track of patterns in what they hear.

cards.headline: Tuned to home
cards.body: Young infants can tell apart many speech sounds, whatever language they hear at home. In a 1981 study led by Janet Werker, 7-month-olds told apart two pairs of Hindi speech sounds, while English-speaking adults had trouble with the rarer pair. Patricia Kuhl has proposed a reason: the brain commits early to the sound patterns it experiences, which might explain why infants learn language better than adults.

cards.headline: Earlier is easier
cards.body: Age keeps mattering after infancy. In 1989, Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport tested the English grammar of 46 Korean and Chinese speakers who had moved to the United States between ages 3 and 39. The earlier people arrived, the better they scored, right up to puberty. After that, scores were low, varied widely and no longer tracked arrival age. When it comes to grammar, earlier really was easier.

questions.prompt: Match each language researcher with who they tested.

pairs.right: Two pairs of Hindi speech sounds

questions.explanation: Jenny Saffran's team tested 8-month-old infants. Janet Werker's study used two pairs of Hindi speech sounds. Johnson and Newport tested 46 Korean and Chinese speakers.

questions.prompt: How did the 8-month-olds in Saffran's study find words in fluent speech?

options.label: By hearing pauses between the words
options.rationale: The only clue was which sounds followed which.

options.label: By watching the speaker point at objects
options.rationale: The clue was in the sounds themselves.

options.label: By practicing the words out loud
By tracking which sounds tended to follow which

questions.explanation: The infants used statistics: which sounds tended to follow which marked where words were.

questions.prompt: Chomsky argued in Level 6 that language learning doesn't depend on detailed reinforcement. How does Saffran's study fit that point?

options.label: Babies needed praise for every word they found
options.rationale: Nobody rewarded or explained anything to them.

options.label: Babies couldn't learn any words before age 4
It showed behaviorism explains all of language
options.rationale: It showed learning from listening, not from rewards.

options.label: Babies picked out words just by listening

questions.explanation: The infants learned words from 2 minutes of listening, with no rewards, fitting Chomsky's point that language learning doesn't rest on detailed reinforcement.
